description: Dillahunty treats past reports as gradable evidence, arguing that agreement among numerous genuinely competing sources increases confidence when direct empirical verification is unavailable.
critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty’s answer makes his testimony standard comparative rather than dismissive, expressly admitting reports from the empirically inaccessible past while explaining why concordance between numerous competing parties increases confidence. Principal limitation: The example never establishes that Gospel accounts are independent, adversarial, or insulated from common traditions, and his self-correction leaves provenance, genre, and reporter reliability insufficiently specified. Live burden: To reinforce his testimony objection, Dillahunty must apply these criteria to debated sources, distinguish numerical plurality from evidential independence, and demonstrate whether cross-party consistency materially improves Christianity’s warrant. Locked score: 82 appropriately rewards the coherent qualification, direct answer, source comparison, and charitable calibration, while comparatively weaker precision and evidential support reflect missing Gospel-level application and unresolved dependence questions.
